issues.item: Triggers: Feeling Happy: Feeling happy or relaxed
issues.explanation: The trigger pattern is not very coherent for a captivity presentation as written: time-of-day could fit, but 'feeling happy or relaxed' and especially 'talks or photos about snakes' imply very different trigger themes without any supporting memory or appraisal content linking them to the captivity trauma.

issues.item: Triggers: Animal Phobia: Talks or photos about snakes
issues.explanation: Threat items mainly describe interpersonal pursuit/external danger (hypervigilance, checking if someone is following me, unsafe at night). That could fit captivity, but it is not well matched to the selected snake-related trigger or to body-monitoring for injury, producing a fragmented threat picture.

issues.item: Threat: Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me
issues.explanation: 'I am not sure my life is worth living anymore' is much more severe and somewhat qualitatively different from the other negative appraisal items, which focus on helplessness and being unable to cope with trauma thoughts. It may occur in PTSD, but here it is weakly integrated with the rest of the selected items.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Life Not Worth Living: I am not sure my life is worth living anymore
issues.explanation: 'Constantly check body for signs of danger or injury' fits health/injury threat, but the threat items emphasize pursuit and ambush, while the triggers emphasize time-of-day, relaxation, and snakes. This coping strategy is therefore poorly linked to the rest of the formulation and symptom pattern.

vignette:
Raj is a 64-year-old warehouse worker who was abducted three years ago while leaving his shift late at night. His captors held him for six hours in a dark, abandoned storage unit, and at one point they threw a burlap sack over his head that he later learned had held snakes-the slithering sensation against his neck was so vivid that even now, the mere mention of a snake in casual conversation makes his stomach drop. The abduction ended when police arrived, but for Raj the night never truly ended.

In the months afterward, Raj began to notice that the same time each evening-around 10:30 PM, when his ordeal began-his body would tense, his heart would race, and he would feel an urgent need to check the locks on every door. He found it harder to feel safe at night than during the day, and he started scanning his surroundings constantly, especially when walking from his truck to the warehouse entrance. At work, he could not stop looking behind him, convinced someone might be following him even though he knew it made no sense. The nighttime itself became a trigger: waking up in the dark, even in his own bedroom, would send a jolt through him, and he would lie still, listening for sounds that weren't there. He started avoiding going to sleep or lying in the dark, staying up until exhaustion forced him into a chair with the television on low. His wife would find him there at dawn, barely asleep.

To cope, Raj began asking his wife repeatedly-sometimes five or six times a night-"Am I okay? Are we safe?" She would reassure him, but it only quieted the fear for a few minutes. He also started checking his own body several times a day: feeling his arms and legs for any sign of injury, pressing on his ribs where he had been kicked, studying his skin in the bathroom mirror at work. That body monitoring kept the memories close, and each time he checked, he thought, I can't stop bad things from happening to me-a belief that grew stronger with every reassurance he sought and every sleepless hour he endured. Because he had come to believe that he was fundamentally unable to protect himself, every shadowed corner of the warehouse and every unexpected sound at night felt like a confirmation that danger was already closing in. He became certain that if he let himself think about the event in any detail, he would not be able to handle it, so he pushed the thoughts away, but that only made the triggers hit harder. The more he avoided sleep, the more he ended up awake in the dark, reliving the moment the sack was pulled over his head. The more he asked for reassurance, the more he noticed his own vigilance, and the more he checked his body, the more he found signs that something was wrong-a scratch, a bruise, a sore muscle-which sent him back into hypervigilance. A few months ago, Raj started thinking his life was not worth living anymore, though he never told anyone that directly.

Now, Raj is seeking help because his wife told him she can't keep doing the nighttime checks, and his supervisor warned him about distracted behavior on the loading dock. What frightens Raj most is the thought that if he stops checking and scanning, he will be caught off guard again. He hopes that talking to someone might help him sleep through a single night without the dark feeling like a cage.
